name: Social-engineering scenario analysis
theory_paragraphs: \term{Social engineering} is the class of attacks that exploit \imp{human behavior rather than system vulnerabilities}. It is the entry point of a large share of real attacks: goals include espionage, direct or indirect access to resources (modern trend: ransomware), data theft and identity theft. Everyone is susceptible, and getting phished reflects the attacker's manipulativeness, not the victim's intelligence. A typical engagement follows the \term{attack phases}: research, pretexting (develop rapport and trust), get the data by exploiting that trust, keep the connection alive, combine data from many small sources, and finally use it.

The course names a toolbox of \term{manipulation strategies}, each exploiting a specific \term{human trait}:
\begin{tightitem}
\item \term{Pretexting / trappings of the role}: fake caller ID, hold music, case numbers, official-looking logos, lookalike domains --- exploits \term{attribution/trust} (we trust what looks like the role).
\item \term{Threat / fear}: 'your account is being emptied', 'a fine will be issued' --- exploits \term{reduced cognitive ability} under fear.
\item \term{Urgency / rush}: deadlines ('within 24 hours', 'before the window closes') --- exploits reduced systematic thinking under time pressure.
\item \term{Rapport / light banter / empathy}: small talk, shared interests --- exploits \term{liking}: people agree to more from someone they like.
\item \term{Peer pressure / social proof}: 'your neighbours already donated' --- exploits the desire not to deviate from social expectations.
\item \term{Altercasting}: forcing the target into a role (helper, victim); e.g. creating a problem and then 'fixing' it --- exploits \term{reactance} and the desire to be helpful/cooperative; fixing builds gratitude and trust.
\end{tightitem}

Further techniques: build credibility, distract from systematic thinking, momentum of compliance, bury questions, read the victim's openness, back off without burning the source, and \imp{aggregate small pieces of data from different sources} into a complete picture (e.g. partial personnummer completed via a public directory lookup). Technical aids include look-alike domains (paypa1.com, junk subdomains), browser-in-the-browser popups, deepfakes, and HTML/JS fake sites. Countermeasures split into \term{organizational} (clear enforced protocols, awareness training, simple rules for what is sensitive, ID required for restricted actions, data classification, culture where 'no' is acceptable) and \term{technical} (phishing filters, 2FA, least privilege, separation of duty, patching).
theory_cheatsheet: Strategy--trait pairs to memorize: trappings of role $\rightarrow$ attribution/trust; fear/threat $\rightarrow$ reduced cognitive ability; urgency $\rightarrow$ no systematic thinking under time pressure; rapport/banter $\rightarrow$ liking; peer pressure $\rightarrow$ desire to conform; altercasting (created-and-fixed problem, helper role) $\rightarrow$ reactance/helpfulness.
Attack phases: research, pretext, get data, keep connection, combine data, use it.
Grading template: each strategy is scored as a triple (strategy name + human trait + quoted scenario line).
Answer part (b) with only what the scenario's final state proves the attacker got; \imp{over-claiming loses the point}.
Part (c) follow-ons: malware from the opened attachment, money from a confirmed transfer, account takeover without 2FA, identity theft where a personnummer alone suffices, credential reuse.
Technical tells of the pretext: lookalike domains (digit-for-letter), spoofed caller ID, 'we never send links' disclaimers, hold music, case/order numbers.
identify_givens: A detailed narrative/transcript of a scam: an attacker (phishing email/SMS, vishing phone call, fake charity/company/bank) contacts a named victim, with quoted attacker lines, victim actions (clicking, entering credentials, opening attachments, confirming with BankID/PayPal), and the final state of what was revealed or executed. Often mentions public data sources the attacker combined (hitta.se, hemnet.se) and lookalike domains (paypa1.com, gmaill.com).
identify_target: (a) Identify ~3 manipulation strategies, name the human trait each exploits, and quote/mention the exact scenario lines supporting each; (b) state concretely what the attacker obtained; (c) give two examples of what the attacker can do now (follow-on attacks).
identify_keywords: quote or mention the parts of the scenario
what can the attacker do now
strategy_name: Strategy-trait-quote triangulation, then concrete harvest and follow-on attacks

algorithm.action: Map each move to a named strategy
algorithm.detail: Label each move with the course's strategy vocabulary: \term{pretext} (trappings of the role), \term{altercasting} (putting the victim into a victim or helper role, e.g. create-then-fix a problem), \term{urgency/rush}, \term{threat/fear}, \term{peer pressure/social proof}, \term{rapport/empathy/light banter}.

For each strategy-trait pair, quote or precisely reference the supporting scenario line (e.g. 'the payment has already come through' for fear). \imp{Deliver full triples: strategy, trait, quote.} The rubric typically awards one point per element, so a strategy without its trait or quote forfeits most of its points.

Enumerate only what the transcript's final state proves the attacker obtained: opened/executed attachment, credentials entered on the lookalike site, full personnummer or other PII, a confirmed BankID/PayPal transfer, phone number. Do not list anything not evidenced in the story --- \imp{one true gain suffices, but any incorrect claim loses the point}.

Provide two realistic next steps consistent with the harvest: hidden malware in the attachment (ransomware, credential stealer) even if payment is refused; money if a transfer was confirmed; initiating further transactions the victim is groomed to confirm; account takeover where no 2FA exists; identity theft at services where a personnummer alone suffices as authentication; credential reuse on other sites.

variations.name: Callback phishing (vishing) instead of an inbound link
variations.detail: The initial email carries no link or attachment; the victim is lured into calling the attacker's number and the attack happens live by phone, with any attachment arriving in a later 'form' mail. Treat hold music, 'we never include links' disclaimers and marketing style as role trappings, and note the extra harvest channel: spoken partial personnummer completed via a public directory lookup. Trap: do not claim the first email itself carried malware.

variations.name: Charity/donation scam with social proof
variations.detail: The lever is peer pressure ('the neighbours have already donated') plus an urgency deadline and a helper-role pretext ('people are suffering'). Name social proof and altercasting instead of fear; the harvest is payment credentials via a lookalike redirect (letter swapped for a digit). Trap: explicitly notice the domain substitution as part of the pretext.

variations.name: Grading granularity of part (a)
variations.detail: Typical rubric: 3 strategies x (strategy + trait + quote), one point each. Strategies without trait or quote forfeit two-thirds of the points; more than three triples is fine since sample answers list 4--5 acceptable options. Always write full triples.

variations.name: What-counts-as-harvest trap in part (b)
variations.detail: Official solutions mark part (b) correct if at least one true gain is mentioned and no incorrect ones --- over-claiming ('got the money' before the BankID confirmation, 'got the password' when only digits were given) loses the point. List only gains explicitly shown in the scenario's final state.

original_problem: Social engineering --- Safe Account: Sara, who lives in Lund, receives an SMS from `PostNord': `Your parcel is held at customs. Pay the SEK 45 fee within 24 hours or it will be returned to the sender.' The link leads to postn0rd.se, a pixel-perfect copy of the real PostNord site, where Sara enters her debit-card number, expiry date and CVV. Two days later her phone rings; the display shows her bank's official support number. `Mikael from the fraud department' greets her warmly, asks how the weather is in Lund, and jokes about the rain he biked through that morning. He then says several customers in her area were hit this week, that case number FB-22114 has been opened, and that two suspicious transactions totalling SEK 14 500 are pending on her account: `if we do not act within the hour, the account will be emptied.' He asks Sara to state her full personnummer `so I can be sure it is really you', then instructs her to move her savings to a `shielded safe account' the bank has created for her, adding the new account as a payee in her banking app. Sara confirms the SEK 12 000 transfer by scanning the QR code with BankID, and Mikael thanks her: `you have been most helpful --- together we caught the thief.' (a) Identify 3 strategies used by the social engineer; for each, name the human trait exploited and quote the parts of the scenario you refer to. (b) What did the attacker get? (c) Give two examples of what the attacker can do now.

original_steps.work: Inventory the moves: fake PostNord SMS with a 24-hour deadline; lookalike domain postn0rd.se (digit `0' for letter `o'); spoofed bank caller ID plus a case number (FB-22114) and a `fraud department' title; small talk about Lund's weather and biking through rain; `several customers in your area were hit'; fear hook (SEK 14 500 pending, `account emptied within the hour'); a created crisis that Mikael then `fixes'; closing flattery (`together we caught the thief').

Name the strategies (any three of): 1) pretext: trappings of the role; 2) threat/fear; 3) urgency/rush; 4) rapport/light banter; 5) peer pressure/social proof; 6) altercasting into helper role (create-and-fix a problem).

Attach the human traits: role trappings exploit attribution/trust; fear and urgency exploit reduced cognitive ability under stress and time pressure; rapport exploits liking (people agree to more from someone they like); social proof exploits the desire not to deviate from what others do; the helper-role ending exploits helpfulness and gratitude/reactance.

Quote the evidence: role trappings --- `the display shows her bank's official support number', `case number FB-22114', `pixel-perfect copy ... postn0rd.se'; fear/urgency --- `pay within 24 hours or it will be returned', `if we do not act within the hour, the account will be emptied'; rapport --- `asks how the weather is in Lund, and jokes about the rain he biked through'; social proof --- `several customers in your area were hit'; helper role --- `together we caught the thief'. Any three full triples earn full marks.

(b) The attacker got: Sara's full debit-card details (number, expiry, CVV) entered on postn0rd.se; her full personnummer; and a BankID-confirmed SEK 12 000 transfer to the attacker's `safe account' (plus the small SEK 45 fee charged to the card). List only these --- not, e.g., her banking password, which was never requested.

(c) Follow-on attacks (any two): use or sell the card details for card-not-present fraud; empty further accounts via repeated `safe account' calls while the grooming holds; commit identity theft --- take loans or order goods at services where a personnummer plus card data suffices as authentication; target Sara again (or her contacts) since she is now a proven compliant victim, e.g. with a `refund' lure that installs malware.
